stem: Which of these is a **straight** fertiliser?

options.content: Ammonium nitrate
options.rationale: Correct: it supplies only nitrogen of the three primary nutrients.

options.content: Compound D (7:14:7)
options.rationale: It supplies N, P and K, so it is a compound fertiliser.

options.content: A 2:3:2 mixture sold for vegetable gardens
options.rationale: It supplies three nutrients, so it is compound.

options.content: Any granular fertiliser that contains nitrogen together with phosphate
options.rationale: Two primary nutrients make it compound.

explanation: A straight fertiliser supplies one primary nutrient: ammonium nitrate (N), single superphosphate (P) or muriate of potash (K).

stem: A bag of fertiliser is labelled 7:14:7. What does the middle number tell you?

options.content: 14% of the fertiliser is phosphate (as P₂O₅)
options.rationale: Correct: the order is always N : P₂O₅ : K₂O.

options.content: 14% of the fertiliser is nitrogen
options.rationale: Nitrogen is the first number, 7.

options.content: The bag contains 14 kg of potash
options.rationale: Potash is the last number, and the numbers are percentages.

options.content: The fertiliser should be applied at 14 kg per hectare
options.rationale: The numbers are an analysis, not a rate.

explanation: The ratio gives percentages by mass of N, P₂O₅ and K₂O, in that order.

stem: Why is nitrogen usually applied as a top dressing rather than all at planting?

options.content: Nitrogen is not needed at all by young seedlings in their first weeks of growth
options.rationale: Seedlings need some nitrogen; basal compounds supply a little.

options.content: Nitrogen fertilisers cannot be bought before the rains
options.rationale: Availability is not the reason.

options.content: It is soluble and easily leached, so it is given when the crop can use it
options.rationale: Correct: late, split doses reduce leaching.

options.content: Nitrogen moves very little in the soil and must be placed on the leaves
options.rationale: Nitrogen moves easily; that is why it leaches.

explanation: Nitrate moves with soil water. Applying it in split doses when the crop is growing fast means less is lost below the roots.

stem: Which method of application is best suited to a wheat crop sown in closely spaced rows?

options.content: Spot placement beside each individual plant
options.rationale: Far too slow for thousands of closely spaced plants.

options.content: Broadcasting
options.rationale: Correct: closely spaced crops cover the whole surface.

options.content: Foliar feeding of all the nitrogen and phosphorus
options.rationale: Foliar feeding suits small doses, such as trace elements.

options.content: Ring placement around each plant
options.rationale: Ring placement suits widely spaced trees.

explanation: Broadcasting spreads fertiliser evenly over the whole field; it suits wheat, pastures and lime.

stem: A farmer drops basal fertiliser directly onto the maize seed in each planting hole. What is the most likely result?

options.content: Faster germination, because the seed gets nutrients sooner
options.rationale: The seed has its own food store; contact with fertiliser harms it.

options.content: No effect at all, because seeds cannot absorb any substances from the soil around them
options.rationale: Seeds absorb water and are damaged by concentrated salts.

options.content: The fertiliser is washed away by the first rain before the seed can use it
options.rationale: Placement in the hole does not wash it away.

options.content: Poor germination: the concentrated salts draw water out of the seed
options.rationale: Correct: this is fertiliser burn.

explanation: Concentrated fertiliser salts lower the water potential around the seed, so water leaves it and it may die. Place fertiliser a few centimetres away and cover it with soil.
hints: Think about osmosis and concentrated salts.

stem: How much nitrogen is contained in one 50 kg bag of a 7:14:7 compound fertiliser?

options.content: 7 kg
options.rationale: 7 is the percentage, not the mass in a 50 kg bag.

options.content: 3.5 kg
14 kg
options.rationale: That is the percentage of phosphate.
This divides 7 by 50 instead of taking 7% of 50.

stem: Why is a trace element such as zinc often applied as a foliar spray?

options.content: Zinc is a gas that must be sprayed onto the crop
options.rationale: Zinc is not a gas.

options.content: Leaves can take up all of the crop's nitrogen and phosphorus needs as well
options.rationale: Large nutrient needs cannot be met through leaves.

options.content: Only a tiny amount is needed and leaves absorb it quickly
options.rationale: Correct: foliar sprays correct trace deficiencies fast.

options.content: Foliar sprays never scorch leaves, however concentrated the solution is
options.rationale: Concentrated sprays do scorch leaves.

explanation: Small doses of trace elements can be absorbed through the leaves, giving a quick correction.
hints: Compare the amounts of trace and major nutrients needed.

stem: Ammonium nitrate is stored in the same shed as diesel and dry grass. What is the main hazard?

options.content: The diesel will turn the fertiliser into a weedkiller
options.rationale: Diesel does not convert fertiliser into herbicide.

options.content: The dry grass will absorb all the nitrogen from the bags
options.rationale: Grass does not absorb nitrogen from bags.

options.content: Fire, because ammonium nitrate is an oxidising substance
options.rationale: Correct: it makes fuels burn fiercely.

options.content: The fertiliser will slowly lose its colour and become useless to crops
options.rationale: Colour is not the concern.

explanation: Store ammonium nitrate dry, on pallets, away from fuels, organic material and naked flames.
hints: What does an oxidising substance do near a fuel?

stem: Basal dressing is fertiliser applied at or just before planting.
explanation: True. Basal dressing, mainly P and K, is applied at planting; top dressing is applied to the growing crop.

stem: Top dressing should be applied to wet leaves so that it dissolves quickly.
explanation: False. Fertiliser on wet leaves scorches them. Apply it to moist soil beside the plants.

stem: Match each method of fertiliser application with its description.

right.content: Sprayed on the leaves as a dilute solution
A measured amount put in each planting hole or station
Placed in a strip along the row, beside and below the seed
Placed beside the rows of a growing crop

explanation: Match the method to where and how the fertiliser is put.

stem: Complete the sentence.

payload.template: Ammonium nitrate contains about {{blank:a}}% nitrogen, and urea contains about {{blank:b}}% nitrogen.

explanation: Ammonium nitrate about 34.5% N; urea about 46% N.

stem: A farmer will apply Compound D at 300 kg/ha to 1.6 ha. How many 50 kg bags must be bought? Round UP to whole bags.
explanation: 300 × 1.6 = 480 kg; 480 ÷ 50 = 9.6, so 10 bags. Rounding down to 9 leaves part of the field without fertiliser.
workedSolution: 1. 300 × 1.6 = 480 kg; 480 ÷ 50 = 9.6, so 10 bags. Rounding down to 9 leaves part of the field without fertiliser.

stem: A vegetable plot measures 60 m by 45 m. Calculate the mass of fertiliser needed at 400 kg/ha, in kg.
explanation: Area = 60 × 45 = 2,700 m² = 0.27 ha. Fertiliser = 400 × 0.27 = 108 kg. Multiplying by the area in m² gives an answer 10,000 times too big.
workedSolution: 1. Area = 60 × 45 = 2,700 m² = 0.27 ha. Fertiliser = 400 × 0.27 = 108 kg. Multiplying by the area in m² gives an answer 10,000 times too big.
hints: Convert the area to hectares first: 1 ha = 10,000 m².

stem: Maize is planted at 75 cm between rows and 25 cm within the row, one plant per station. Ammonium nitrate is to be side-dressed at 250 kg/ha. Calculate the mass of ammonium nitrate per plant, in g, to one decimal place.
workedSolution:
1. Area per plant = 0.75 m × 0.25 m = 0.1875 m².
2. Plants per hectare = 10,000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53,333.
3. Fertiliser per hectare in grams = 250 × 1,000 = 250,000 g.
4. Per plant = 250,000 ÷ 53,333 = 4.7 g.
hints: Find the plants per hectare first.
Convert kg to g before dividing.

stem: A crop needs 69 kg of nitrogen per hectare. Assume urea contains 46% N. Calculate the mass of urea needed per hectare, in kg.
explanation: Urea = 69 ÷ 0.46 = 150 kg/ha. Multiplying 69 by 0.46 (31.74 kg) gives the nitrogen in 69 kg of urea instead.
workedSolution:
1. Each kg of urea contains 0.46 kg N.
2. Urea needed = 69 ÷ 0.46 = 150 kg/ha.
3. Check: 150 × 0.46 = 69 kg N.
hints: Divide the nitrogen needed by the fraction of nitrogen in urea.

stem: A soya bean crop needs 45 kg of P₂O₅ per hectare from single superphosphate. Assume single superphosphate contains 18% P₂O₅. Calculate the mass of single superphosphate needed per hectare, in kg.
explanation: 45 ÷ 0.18 = 250 kg/ha. Multiplying 45 by 0.18 gives the P₂O₅ in 45 kg of fertiliser instead.
workedSolution: 1. 45 ÷ 0.18 = 250 kg/ha. Multiplying 45 by 0.18 gives the P₂O₅ in 45 kg of fertiliser instead.

stem: Calculate the mass of nitrogen applied when 300 kg of Compound D (7:14:7) is spread on one hectare, in kg.
explanation: N = 300 × 7 ÷ 100 = 21 kg. Using 14% (the phosphate figure) gives 42 kg.
workedSolution: 1. N = 300 × 7 ÷ 100 = 21 kg. Using 14% (the phosphate figure) gives 42 kg.

stem: Name the straight fertiliser that supplies potassium and contains about 60% K₂O.
explanation: **Muriate of potash** (potassium chloride).

stem: Distinguish between basal dressing and top dressing of maize.

points.description: Basal dressing is applied at or just before planting.
It supplies mainly phosphorus and potassium (e.g. Compound D) for root and early growth.
Top dressing is applied to the growing crop after emergence (often split).
It supplies mainly nitrogen (e.g. ammonium nitrate), which is easily leached, when the crop needs it most.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Basal dressing is put on at planting and supplies mainly phosphorus and potassium, for example Compound D, which help root growth and move little in the soil. Top dressing is put on the growing maize after emergence, often in two splits, and supplies mainly nitrogen such as ammonium nitrate, because nitrogen leaches easily and is needed most during rapid leafy growth.

explanation: Compare timing, nutrients and reason.
hints: Compare when, which nutrients and why.

stem:
Rudo plans to grow 0.8 ha of maize near Marondera. Her fertiliser programme is shown below. Fertiliser is sold in 50 kg bags.

| Fertiliser | Analysis (assume) | Rate (kg/ha) | When applied |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Compound D | N:P:K compound, 7% N | 400 | At planting |
| Ammonium nitrate | 34.5% N | 250 | Split: 4 and 7 weeks after emergence |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bags of Compound D she must buy. Round UP to whole bags.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of bags of ammonium nitrate she must buy.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the total mass of nitrogen applied per hectare from both fertilisers, in kg, to two decimal places.
parts.explanation: Compound D: 400 × 7 ÷ 100 = 28 kg; ammonium nitrate: 250 × 34.5 ÷ 100 = 86.25 kg; total 114.25 kg N/ha.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Compound D: 400 × 7 ÷ 100 = 28 kg; ammonium nitrate: 250 × 34.5 ÷ 100 = 86.25 kg; total 114.25 kg N/ha.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Which method is best for applying the Compound D at planting?

options.content: Foliar spraying onto the young leaves after the crop has emerged
options.rationale: Basal fertiliser is applied at planting, in the soil.

options.content: Broadcasting on the soil surface six weeks after planting
options.rationale: That is too late for a basal dressing.

options.content: Mixing it with the seed in the planter box before sowing
options.rationale: Contact with the seed can burn it.

options.content: Banding or placement near, but not touching, the seed
options.rationale: Correct: P and K move little, so they are placed near the roots.

parts.explanation: Basal fertiliser is banded or placed a few centimetres from the seed and covered.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why the ammonium nitrate is split into two applications.

points.description: Nitrate is soluble and easily leached by heavy rain.
Smaller doses when the crop is growing fast mean more is taken up and less is lost / wasted.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe **three** precautions Rudo should take when storing the fertiliser.

points.description: Keep it dry under a roof, on pallets off the floor (prevents caking).
Keep it away from seed, food, feed and pesticides.
Keep ammonium nitrate away from fuels, straw and flames (fire risk) / keep children and animals away.

parts.explanation: Dry, separate and away from fire.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: State **one** sign on the maize that would show the top dressing was too little.

points.description: Yellowing of the older, lower leaves (V-shape along the midrib) / pale, stunted plants.

explanation: Bags = rate × area ÷ 50 (round up); nutrients = product × %; then method, timing and storage.
hints: kg = rate × area; bags are rounded up.

stem: Farai grows cabbages under drip irrigation in a garden near Mutare. His neighbour broadcasts all his fertiliser by hand over the whole garden before planting, and many weeds grow between the rows.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Name the method of applying fertiliser dissolved in the drip irrigation water.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain **three** advantages of Farai's method over the neighbour's.

points.description: Nutrients go straight to the root zone of the crop, not to weeds between rows.
Small, frequent doses match the crop's needs, so less is leached / wasted.
Saves labour / even distribution / no fertiliser burn from concentrated granules.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: State **two** disadvantages of broadcasting fertiliser for widely spaced row crops.

points.description: Much fertiliser falls between rows where it feeds weeds.
More is needed / wasted / lost by leaching or runoff.

explanation: Placement methods put nutrients where the crop's roots are.
hints: Who uses the fertiliser when it is broadcast?
